sentences.text: This footage is from Iran state television, so take it with a grain of salt, but it claims to show an underground drone manufacturing facility with the military saying there's more as the country expands production.
It's meant to signal in part that Iran has been building its stockpile back up during the past few months of relative quiet in the Middle East war.
Tehran is ready should fighting resume in a big way.
That is the message, at least.

Another message on Thursday, Iran also claimed that it struck seven oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, which, if true, would be the largest single-day hit in the strait since the start of the war in late February.
US President Donald Trump, however, called those claims fake, saying the regime is intentionally driving up the price of oil ahead of the US midterm elections.

Now, there are a number of indicators that the fighting might pick back up after Americans vote on November 3rd from the New York Times, US and Israel draw up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after elections.
It doesn't get more explicit than that.
And the Wall Street Journal says quote, Iran threatens wider strikes on economic and civilian targets if U.S. attacks.
The Guardian reports on how Iran will hit AI facilities across the Gulf if the fighting resumes.
There have been other clues, including US Secretary of Defense Pete Heggseth's visit to Israel earlier this week, where he met Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Keep in mind that Israel also has elections happening in just a matter of days.
So for both the US and Israel, everything after the election.
To dive into all this, we have military analyst Sean Bell joining us.
Sean, uh first off, has there been any other verification beyond what Tehran says that Iran did indeed hit seven oil tankers?
Great to join you.
No, there hasn't.
And as we've had ever since the 28th of February, when America launched its waves of attack against Iran, this has largely become a war of the narrative.
And where we find ourselves, you you quoted that it actually had been relatively quiet for a few weeks.
Well, part of that is the run-up to the midterm elections.
But part of it is both sides have hit a bit of a stalemate.
The one thing that's not been widely reported is the US is providing escorts to oil coming through the Strait of Hormuz, but the US blockade of Iranian oil exports remains pretty robust.
So the stemate doesn't suit Iran at all.
And that's why they've been fueling arming the Houthi rebels and trying to cause havoc at the bottom of the Baba Mandab straits and the Red Sea.
So what we're seeing at the moment is a bit of a lull, which doesn't suit either side, and that's why the oil prices remain stubbornly high at record levels, certainly in the UK.
We'll talk about the Houthis in a little bit.
It's a very interesting what's been happening, of course, with the Houthis and with Saudi Arabia.
Now, whether these uh oil tanker strikes happened or not, uh, it is, as you say, something about the narrative.

Uh, now, along with the release of the video showing that its military is uh uh is is building these drones, uh the Iran is also saying that it's stocking up weapons, as you said, it's been a relatively quiet time.

To what extent do you think it can, given the limited resources of Iran, given that uh even before the start of the war, its economy uh was in the doldrums and kind of uh in many uh people's opinion, kind of it's on its last legs.
How can it stock up weapons?
Yeah, it's interesting, isn't it?
We tend to look at these problems through a Western lens.
Um, that our economy is based, you know, on a on a um a democratic system.
We have to remember in Iran, it's an autocratic system.
The leadership have stowed money away for years.
There's no doubt I have friends who have relations in Iran, and they say life is very difficult there indeed.
But that hasn't stopped the Iranian leadership having plenty of money and facilities to actually make these weapons.
It's also worth noting that although there's a blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, there's lots of land routes that provide resupply in to Iran.
So they're not short of getting kids and equipment in.
The other point I would make is um, and this is not being a smart ass about the whole situation.
But when I was in the military, we used to war game this sort of scenario.
I have played Iran in those war games.
And the might of America always prevails over the conventional Iranian forces.
But Iran has prepared for this day to be able to control the Strait of Hormuz with drones, with anti-ship missiles, with uh fast patrol boats and mines.

They're all very well hidden, they're very well supplied, and even though America has had a very successful military campaign, most analysts believe Iran probably has at least half of its ballistic missiles left and many thousands of drones.
So the America has won the conventional battle, beaten up Iran's air, land and maritime, but around the Strait of Hormuz, um the Iranian capability is still very dangerous.
Sean, I'd love your take on what Trump will do.
Um, once public opinion matters less after the elections.
We, for example, have seen that the US has moved another aircraft carrier into the region in recent weeks.
What do you think will happen?
Well, I know the conjecture is all that there'll be a big increase in military action again, but you have to go back to the start of this war.
President Trump claimed within four to six weeks the war would be over, that he would have won, that America's superpower would have devastated Iran.
And in many respects it did.
But ever since then, it has proven that America's been incapable of actually stopping Iran controlling the Strada Formuz.
And even if America was to return to a military campaign, it looks very unlikely that there would be any difference to the military campaign that was before.
And the bad side is that Iran has learnt from that experience.
It has been targeting Saudi Arabia and targeting US military facilities in the Middle East.

That has caused a great deal of difficulty for America's allies in the region, and also means that things like patriot missile systems are vital to protect against those ballistic missiles are now running in really short supply.
In short, what I'm saying is that there is no military answer to this predicament.
If President Trump decides to revert back to using the military, it isn't going to change the game.
All we are going to see is a lot more uproar from the Middle East.
And I think that's why the Middle East are looking at where do they get their relationships in the future?
Because their America is clearly wavering as a key supporter of its national security.
I want to talk a little bit about the American stockpile that you referenced there.
Um, because of course we've just been focusing on what the Iranians have been doing, building up the drones uh manufacturing and stockpiling uh during this interregnum.
Um, but uh Americans have also been running out of pretty expensive weapons.
Uh do you have a sense of how much it's been able to replenish of its own resources?
Well, there's little doubt that we're hearing already that um supplies of weapons that were being bought by NATO by NATO countries to provide to Ukraine.
Um, Pete Hex said that's been very public and saying, well, we're not providing those.
I know they NATO's paid for them, but we have to prioritize getting our own stockpiles sorted first.
So it's having an impact on the ability of NATO to support Ukraine and stop the Russian aggression.
But I think more importantly, things like patriot.
We're gonna pick on Patriot for a minute because um the ballistic missile threat from Iran is significant for every one ballistic missile fired, you generally fire two patriots.
The system in America, the industry can only actually replace Patriots at two a day.
Well, it therefore that's only one ballistic missile a day, and all of a sudden that day's supply of patriots is used up.
When we're in the war, regularly there will be a dozen ballistic missiles fired, 24 patriots.
That's just not sustainable.
And of course, Iran knows it.
So the danger here is that America won't run out of its ability to strike Iran.
What it will do is it will struggle to help the Middle East protect itself.
And that will be incredibly dangerous, very unpopular, and will cause America a great deal of diplomatic difficulty in the region.
Let's talk a little bit about the rest of the Middle East.
You uh mentioned the Houthis earlier in Yemen and Saudi Arabia.
They have been trading fire.
Where do things stand there and how does that fighting fit into the larger uh Middle East conflict?
Yeah, it is interesting.
I mean, the Houthis and Saudi Arabia have been involved in a conflict for many years, but it sort of subsided a few years ago and sort of bubbles along because the Houthis were very ill-equipped.
Saudi was much better equipped, and although it was an irritation, it wasn't something that was really causing the Saudis too much problem.
But of course, the Houthis as well as Hamas and Hezbollah are all uh proxies of Iran.

When Iran got stuck in this stalemate around the Strait of Hormuz, they've been providing a lot of high grade weapons to the Houthis, and they've therefore been able to terrorize the Bab al-Mandab straits.
They've also been able to use drones and ballistic missiles, weapons they didn't have before, that are actually therefore able to kill a lot of people tragically in Saudi Arabia.
Why have they targeted Saudi Arabia in particular?

Because Saudi had spent a lot of its oil revenue trying to wean itself off dependence on the Strait of Hormuz by building a massive pipeline from the east side of the country to the west, so they could offload oil into the Red Sea and therefore use the Baba Mandab Straits.
Now the Houthis are targeting that, all of which designed to make life uncomfortable, push energy prices high, and put more pressure onto Donald Trump.
That's what's happening with Yemen at the moment, and that's why the Houthis are so dangerous equipped with high-tech weapons provided by Iran.
Sean, we talked a lot uh about uh the kinetics so far.
So let's switch uh to the diplomatic.
Um, how all of this develops is of course important globally, and we're seeing this uh with a kind of diplomacy happening.

For example, uh, today, as we speak, it is uh Friday, the foreign ministers of the UK, France, Germany, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Egypt are meeting in Istanbul, and that's the meeting of the E3 with the R4, to use the jargon.
How significant is this meeting?
It's very significant, and I think there's lots going on behind the scenes.
If you look at this grand strategically, for many decades, America and the UK and other nations provided strategic security guarantors to the Middle East in return for oil.
In other words, oil for arms.
Now that's prevailed for many years, but when America suddenly struck Iran, they didn't talk to Saudi Arabia.
They didn't talk to Qatar, they didn't talk to the UA
